title: The Responsibility Chart
summary: On Sunday evening, Omar's mother sat down with him to plan the week ahead.
text:
On Sunday evening, Omar's mother sat down with him to plan the week ahead.
"Omar," she said, pointing to the responsibility chart on the fridge, "these are your jobs for this week. Making your bed every morning, putting your laundry in the hamper, and feeding the cat before dinner."
Omar looked at the chart. "Do I have to do all of them every single day?"
"Yes," said his mother. "These aren't chores I'm asking you to do — they're responsibilities you own. That means no reminders from me. The chart does the reminding."
Omar sighed. "But what if I forget?"
"Then you'll experience what happens when responsibilities don't get done," said his mother calmly. "If the bed isn't made, you'll sleep in an unmade bed that night. If the laundry isn't in the hamper, it won't get washed. If the cat isn't fed, she'll be hungry — and that's not fair to her."
Omar nodded slowly. He understood.
Monday morning, Omar made his bed without being asked. Tuesday, he remembered the laundry. Wednesday, he fed the cat right after school.
But Thursday morning, he rushed out the door without making his bed.
That night, when he came home from school, his bed was still unmade.
"Mom," he said, "can you help me make my bed now?"
His mother shook her head gently. "You can make it yourself. And tonight, you'll sleep in whatever condition your bed is in when you go to bed."
Omar felt frustrated, but he knew his mother was right. He made the bed quickly, but it wasn't as neat as usual.
That night, sleeping in the slightly messy bed, Omar realized something: making his bed in the morning took two minutes. But fixing it at night, when he was tired, took ten minutes and felt much harder.
The next morning, he made his bed without thinking twice.
By Friday, Omar's mother noticed the change. "You've been doing all your responsibilities without reminders," she observed. "How does that feel?"
Omar thought about it. "Actually... kind of good. Like I'm capable. Like I don't need you to remind me about everything."
"That's exactly right," said his mother. "Responsibility isn't about doing what I tell you. It's about owning what needs to be done, whether I'm there or not."
Omar nodded, feeling proud. The chart wasn't a list of punishments — it was a map showing him what he was capable of handling on his own.
lesson: Responsibility isn't about obeying parent commands — it's about owning tasks that need to be done, whether anyone is watching or not; natural consequences (sleeping in an unmade bed) teach more effectively than punishments or reminders.
grammarFocus: Reported speech for parent-child dialogue ("she said these were his jobs"); future forms for natural consequences ("you'll sleep," "it won't get washed"); contrast clauses for nuanced explanation ("whether I'm there or not"); question tags for gentle confirmation ("That's right, isn't it?"); present perfect for accumulated change ("you've been doing").

Which detail from the story best shows its main lesson? Explain your choice.
